answers.children: Yes — Scottish Deerhounds are exceptionally gentle and patient with family, including children, often resting their massive heads on a child’s lap with tenderness. Their dignified and friendly nature combines with an athletic yet graceful build from coursing deer in the Scottish Highlands, allowing them to tolerate energetic play without becoming overwhelmed. The breed’s size requires careful movement around toddlers to avoid accidental knocks from their long legs. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 7/10)
answers.other-pets: Scottish Deerhounds can get along with other pets when raised together but their high prey drive leads to chasing smaller animals or anything that moves quickly. Bred for coursing deer, their sighthound instincts make them prone to bolt after squirrels, cats or even blowing leaves during walks. With same-size companions they remain friendly and dignified, though supervision helps manage sudden pursuits.
answers.exercise: Scottish Deerhounds need at least an hour a day of activity, ideally including off-leash sprints in a secure area. Built for speed and endurance from coursing deer across rough Scottish terrain, a few minutes of full-out galloping in open fields tires them more effectively than slow walks. Without this outlet the gentle giants become restless despite their laid-back indoor demeanor.
answers.shedding: Yes — Scottish Deerhounds shed moderately with a medium wire coat that produces noticeable hair around the home. The coarse texture and moderate length mean loose hairs cling to furniture and clothing, especially during seasonal changes, while their large athletic build spreads the shedding further when they flop down after activity. Regular brushing helps manage the wire coat’s tendency to trap debris from outdoor runs.
answers.hypoallergenic: Scottish Deerhounds are not hypoallergenic. Their medium wire coat sheds at a low-to-moderate level and produces the dander typical of sighthounds built for the Scottish highlands. The breed is rarely suggested to allergy sufferers because the wiry texture still spreads hair and allergens around the home. No breed is genuinely hypoallergenic.
answers.training: Scottish Deerhounds are not the easiest to train because of their independent sighthound nature bred for chasing deer without constant human direction. Their moderate intelligence and dignified temperament mean they respond best to patient, positive methods rather than repetitive drills, though their affectionate bond with family can aid motivation. The athletic build requires training that channels their graceful speed into reliable recall.
answers.lifespan: Scottish Deerhounds live 8-11 years. Their short lifespan and health concerns stem from the large, athletic build developed for coursing deer over rugged terrain, which places demands on their frame despite the gentle and dignified personality they show at home. The breed’s graceful proportions and substantial weight contribute to the limited years compared with smaller hounds.
answers.size: Scottish Deerhounds reach 75-110 lb and stand 28-32 in tall. Their leggy, towering build allows them to lope with ballet-like grace across fields yet flop onto couches with surprising delicacy for their size, creating a paradoxical feel in the home where their long legs sprawl in every direction. This athletic frame from deer coursing means they take up significant space when resting indoors.
answers.barking: Scottish Deerhounds bark little and tend to stay quiet unless something truly captures their attention. Their dignified and friendly temperament, shaped by centuries of coursing deer in the Scottish Highlands, favours silent pursuit over vocal alerts, so they rarely disturb the household with noise. The gentle giants prefer to observe with a calm, regal stare rather than announce every passing stimulus, making them suitable where excessive barking would be unwelcome. (PawLabs barking score: 3/10)
answers.apartment: No — Scottish Deerhounds do not suit apartment living well because their need for regular sprints and space to stretch long legs conflicts with confined areas. Although they settle indoors with a laid-back, dignified demeanor and low barking, the athletic build from coursing deer demands secure open fields for galloping to prevent restlessness. Their substantial size and tendency to sprawl also make tight quarters impractical.
answers.first-time: No — Scottish Deerhounds are not ideal as a first dog because their high prey drive demands experienced handling to manage sudden chasing instincts. The combination of large athletic size, short lifespan with health concerns, and independent sighthound nature from deer coursing requires an owner who understands how to provide secure exercise and patient training without becoming overwhelmed by the gentle yet strong-willed giant.
